The poll also suggests that most Americans suspect people in Muslim countries don't think highly of the United States. The poll's release comes hours before the president flies to Saudi Arabia for meetings with King Abdullah. Following the stop in Saudi Arabia, Obama will head to Egypt, where he'll deliver a long-awaited speech Thursday on relations between the United States and the Muslim world.  Watch the challenges Obama faces with the speech » . At a town hall in Turkey earlier this year, the president declared that "the United States is not, and will never be, at war with Islam." Many Americans seem to agree with the president: Sixty-two percent of those surveyed say they don't think the United States is at war with the Muslim world, with 36 percent indicating that the country is at war with Muslim countries. Those numbers have remained stable since CNN's 2002 poll. But the poll suggests that six out of 10 think that the Muslim world considers itself at war with the United States. counterfactuals.output:
**Poll: Americans wary of Muslim countries ahead of Obama Mideast trip**

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — As President Barack Obama prepares to travel to Saudi Arabia and Egypt, a new national poll suggests he will be speaking not only to audiences in the Muslim world, but also to an American public that remains deeply divided — and often skeptical — about Muslim countries.

A CNN/Opinion Research Corp. survey released ahead of the trip found that many Americans hold unfavorable views of Muslim countries, underscoring the challenge facing Obama as he seeks to improve U.S. relations with the Islamic world.

The poll indicates that a majority of Americans say they have an unfavorable opinion of Muslim countries, while fewer say their views are favorable. The findings come as Obama plans a major address in Cairo aimed at resetting relations after years of tension over the Iraq war, terrorism, the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and U.S. policy in the Middle East.

Obama is scheduled to visit Saudi Arabia before traveling to Egypt, where the White House says he will deliver a speech intended to “seek a new beginning” between the United States and Muslims around the globe.

The poll suggests public opinion at home could complicate that effort. Views of Muslim countries vary sharply along political lines, with Democrats generally more likely than Republicans to express favorable opinions. Younger Americans also tend to be more open in their views than older Americans, according to the survey.

Still, the poll shows broad interest in improving relations, even among Americans who express reservations. Foreign policy analysts say that gives Obama an opportunity to frame engagement with Muslim-majority nations as both a diplomatic necessity and a matter of national security.

The president has repeatedly argued that the United States is not at war with Islam, but with violent extremists. Since taking office, he has moved to change the tone of U.S. diplomacy, including an interview with an Arab television network and outreach tied to the Persian New Year.

Obama’s Cairo speech is expected to address terrorism, democracy, religious freedom, the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and America’s role in the region. White House officials say the president will acknowledge disagreements while emphasizing mutual respect.

The CNN/Opinion Research Corp. poll was conducted among a national sample of adult Americans and has a margin of sampling error of plus or minus several percentage points.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

According to the CNN/Opinion Research Corp. polling data, Americans were split in their overall views of the Muslim world, with a substantial share holding unfavorable opinions. At the same time, many respondents said relations between the United States and Muslim-majority countries were important to American interests and supported diplomatic efforts to improve them.

The poll also suggested that Obama entered the trip with more public confidence than his predecessor on the issue. Many Americans said they believed Obama’s approach could help improve U.S. relations with Muslims abroad, though skepticism remained about whether deeper differences between the United States and the Muslim world could be overcome.

Obama’s Middle East visit was intended to signal a shift in tone from the Bush administration, emphasizing mutual respect, dialogue and cooperation on issues such as extremism, the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, Iran and economic development. His speech in Cairo was framed by the White House as a cornerstone of that outreach.

The polling underscored the challenge facing the president: while Americans appeared open to a new diplomatic approach, public attitudes toward the Muslim world were still shaped by security concerns, cultural mistrust and years of conflict.

The CNN/Opinion Research Corp. survey was conducted among a national sample of U.S. adults and carried a margin of sampling error of roughly plus or minus 3 percentage points.

**Poll: One in Five Americans View Muslim Countries Favorably Ahead of Obama Speech in Egypt**

**WASHINGTON** — As President Barack Obama prepares to deliver a closely watched address in Egypt aimed at improving relations between the United States and the Muslim world, a new poll finds that only about one in five Americans view Muslim countries favorably.

The survey underscores the challenge facing Obama as he seeks to reset U.S. ties with Muslim-majority nations after years of tension fueled by the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, concerns over terrorism, and widespread mistrust on both sides.

Obama is scheduled to speak in Cairo, where White House officials say he will outline a new approach based on “mutual interest and mutual respect.” The speech is expected to address issues including extremism, the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, democracy, religious freedom and economic development.

The poll’s findings suggest that many Americans remain skeptical of Muslim-majority countries, even as the administration attempts to broaden diplomatic engagement. Analysts say public opinion at home could shape how much political room Obama has to pursue a different course in the region.

“This speech is not just directed at audiences overseas,” one foreign policy analyst said. “It is also a message to Americans that the United States has strategic and moral reasons to rebuild relationships with Muslim communities.”

Obama has repeatedly said the United States is not at war with Islam, a theme he is expected to emphasize in Egypt. His administration has also sought to distinguish its counterterrorism efforts from broader relations with Muslim populations around the world.

The Cairo address will be one of Obama’s most significant foreign policy speeches since taking office. Expectations are high across the Middle East, where many are looking for signs of concrete changes in U.S. policy, particularly on the Israeli-Palestinian peace process and America’s military presence in the region.

Still, White House officials have cautioned that the speech is only a first step.

“No single address can erase years of mistrust,” an administration official said. “But the president believes it is important to begin with an honest conversation.”

The poll indicates that Obama may face a difficult balancing act: reaching out to Muslim-majority nations while reassuring Americans concerned about security and U.S. interests abroad.

Whether the speech changes perceptions — either in the United States or overseas — may depend less on Obama’s words in Cairo than on the policies that follow.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a 2009-era CNN article about President Obama traveling to the Middle East, American attitudes toward Muslim countries, and whether Americans think the U.S. is at war with Islam.
counterfactuals.output:
**Obama heads to Middle East amid mixed U.S. views of Muslim world**

*By CNN Political Unit*  
*June 2009*

WASHINGTON (CNN) — As President Obama prepares for a closely watched trip to the Middle East, many Americans say they support his effort to improve relations with Muslim-majority countries, but deep doubts remain about the region and about how the United States is perceived there.

Obama’s trip, which includes a major address aimed at Muslims around the world, comes as the administration tries to turn the page from the tensions of the Bush years, the Iraq war and the broader U.S.-led fight against terrorism.

White House officials say the president’s message will be simple: The United States is not at war with Islam.

That point appears to be shared by most Americans, according to recent polling. A majority of Americans say they do not believe the United States is engaged in a war against Islam itself, even as many continue to view some Muslim countries with suspicion and remain concerned about terrorism.

The distinction is central to Obama’s foreign policy approach. Since taking office, he has repeatedly emphasized that the United States is fighting al Qaeda and other extremist groups — not Muslims or the Islamic faith.

“We are not at war with Islam,” Obama said earlier this year, echoing language used by previous administrations but placing it at the center of a broader diplomatic outreach campaign.

The president’s upcoming speech is expected to address several issues that have strained relations between the United States and Muslim communities, including the war in Iraq, the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, Iran’s nuclear ambitions and the U.S. military presence in Afghanistan.

Administration officials say Obama will also highlight his own biography — including his childhood years in Indonesia and his family connections to Muslims — as part of an effort to show respect for Islam and to counter anti-American sentiment abroad.

But at home, the political landscape is complicated.

Many Americans remain wary of governments in the Middle East and South Asia, particularly Iran and Pakistan. Concerns about terrorism continue to shape public opinion, nearly eight years after the September 11 attacks. At the same time, there is broad support for repairing America’s image overseas, especially among Democrats and independents.

Republicans have been more divided. Some GOP lawmakers have welcomed outreach to Muslim allies, while others have warned Obama not to appear apologetic for U.S. actions after September 11.

“The president should speak clearly about American values, but he should not suggest that the United States is to blame for extremism,” one Republican strategist said.

Democrats argue that Obama’s approach is a necessary break from what they describe as the diplomatic damage caused by the Iraq war.

“Engagement is not weakness,” a senior Democratic aide said. “It is a recognition that America’s security depends not only on military power, but also on rebuilding trust.”

Foreign policy analysts say the stakes are high. Obama remains popular in much of Europe and has generated curiosity in parts of the Muslim world, but public opinion in the Middle East remains skeptical of U.S. intentions. Many Muslims abroad want to see policy changes, not just new language.

“A speech can open a door,” said one Middle East analyst. “But the real test will be what happens on Iraq, Afghanistan, Guantanamo, and the Israeli-Palestinian peace process.”

Obama has already ordered the closure of the U.S. detention facility at Guantanamo Bay, though the administration faces resistance in Congress over where to send detainees. He has also announced a drawdown plan for Iraq while increasing the U.S. troop commitment in Afghanistan.

That combination — ending one war while escalating another — could complicate the president’s message.

Still, the White House believes Obama has an opportunity to reset the tone of U.S. relations with Muslim-majority nations at a moment when many Americans are open to a different approach.

For Obama, the challenge will be to reassure audiences abroad that America respects Islam, while convincing Americans at home that outreach does not mean retreating from the fight against terrorism.

As one administration official put it, “The president believes we can be tough on extremists and respectful toward Muslims at the same time.”

counterfactuals.output:
WASHINGTON, June 2 — President Barack Obama heads to Saudi Arabia and Egypt this week seeking to reset relations with the Muslim world, a central foreign-policy objective that comes as polling shows deep skepticism toward the United States across several Muslim-majority countries.

Obama is scheduled to meet Saudi King Abdullah in Riyadh before traveling to Cairo, where he will deliver a major address aimed at Muslims worldwide. The speech is expected to stress “mutual respect,” a phrase Obama has used repeatedly since taking office, while acknowledging disputes over U.S. policy in the Middle East, the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

Public opinion surveys underscore the challenge. A 2008 Pew Global Attitudes survey found favorable views of the United States at 22 percent in Egypt, 19 percent in Jordan and Pakistan, and 12 percent in Turkey. Pew polling also showed confidence in then-President George W. Bush in single digits in several Muslim-majority countries. Gallup surveys during the same period found low approval of U.S. leadership across much of the Middle East and North Africa.

CNN analysts have described the trip as an early test of whether Obama’s personal popularity and rhetorical shift can translate into policy credibility. CNN national security analyst Peter Bergen has noted in past commentary that Obama’s biography and opposition to the Iraq war give him an opening in the region, but that expectations will depend heavily on concrete movement on issues such as Israeli-Palestinian peace, Guantanamo Bay and Afghanistan.

Obama has tried to signal a different tone since his first days in office. In his inaugural address, he told Muslim communities that the United States sought “a new way forward, based on mutual interest and mutual respect.” Days later, in an interview with Al Arabiya, he said his administration would listen as well as lead and emphasized that “Americans are not your enemy.”

The White House says the Cairo speech is intended to reach beyond governments to ordinary Muslims. Officials have said Obama will address violent extremism but also education, economic opportunity and the contributions of Muslim communities.

Analysts caution that symbolism alone is unlikely to repair years of mistrust. The U.S. invasion of Iraq, civilian casualties in conflict zones, support for authoritarian Arab allies and Washington’s close relationship with Israel have all damaged America’s image. Obama’s decision to close the Guantanamo detention facility, his planned withdrawal of combat forces from Iraq and his appointment of a Middle East peace envoy have been welcomed in some quarters, but many in the region are waiting to see results.

In Saudi Arabia, Obama is expected to discuss energy, Iran, counterterrorism and Arab-Israeli diplomacy. In Egypt, his speech will be watched closely not only for what he says about Islam and the West, but also for how directly he addresses democracy and human rights under President Hosni Mubarak, a longtime U.S. ally.

For Obama, the trip offers a chance to recast the tone of U.S. engagement. The harder task, diplomats and regional experts say, will be proving that the change extends beyond words.
